name: Aripiprazole
sections: Melting point 138–150 °C; twelve known crystalline polymorphs.

Approved for schizophrenia in 2002, bipolar mania in 2004, adjunctive treatment of major depressive disorder in 2007 and irritability in autism in 2009. First approval/introduction: US FDA 2002 (schizophrenia); discovered by Otsuka Pharmaceutical in 1988.

Partial agonist at dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT1A receptors and antagonist at 5-HT2A receptors ('dopamine-serotonin system stabiliser'). Reduces dopaminergic over-activity in mesolimbic pathways while preserving activity in mesocortical pathways. Receptor / target profile: Functionally selective partial agonist at D2 (Ki 0.65–4.4 nM, ~60% intrinsic activity); partial agonist at D3, D4, 5-HT1A (Ki 1.7–6.4 nM) and 5-HT2C; antagonist at 5-HT2A.
Hepatic, mostly via CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 (active metabolite dehydro-aripiprazole)
Summary: Oral bioavailability ~87%; Tmax 3–5 h. >99% protein bound. Metabolised by CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 to active dehydro-aripiprazole. Half-life ~75 h (steady state in ~14 days).
Schizophrenia in adults and adolescents (≥15 years)
Acute manic or mixed episodes of bipolar I disorder and maintenance
Adjunctive treatment of major depressive disorder
Irritability associated with autistic disorder; Tourette's disorder (paediatric)
Schizophrenia: start 10–15 mg once daily; usual 10–30 mg/day
Bipolar mania: 15 mg once daily (monotherapy or adjunct), up to 30 mg/day
Adjunct in MDD: 2–5 mg/day, titrate to 5–15 mg/day
Halve dose with strong CYP2D6/3A4 inhibitors; double with strong CYP3A4 inducers
Dose to be individualised by the treating physician according to clinical response and tolerability.
No adjustment (use with caution in severe impairment).
Not approved for dementia-related psychosis; increased mortality and stroke risk.
Approved for schizophrenia (13–17 y), bipolar mania (10–17 y), autism-related irritability (6–17 y), Tourette's (6–18 y) in some regions; monitor for suicidality.
Use only if benefit outweighs risk; third-trimester exposure may cause extrapyramidal/withdrawal symptoms in neonates.
Excreted in breast milk; decide between breastfeeding and therapy.
Increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis
Suicidal thoughts in children, adolescents and young adults (antidepressant use)
Akathisia, tardive dyskinesia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Impulse-control problems (pathological gambling, binge eating, compulsive shopping)
Metabolic changes – monitor glucose, lipids and weight
Strong CYP2D6 inhibitors (fluoxetine, paroxetine) or CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, clarithromycin) – halve the dose
CYP3A4 inducers (carbamazepine, rifampicin) – double the dose
Take with or without food; avoid alcohol and grapefruit juice (CYP3A4).
Weight, BMI, fasting glucose/HbA1c, lipids at baseline and periodically; CBC if history of leucopenia; impulse-control behaviour.
Somnolence, vomiting, tachycardia, EPS. Supportive care; activated charcoal early; ECG monitoring.
Leucht et al., Lancet 2013 – favourable metabolic and prolactin profile among antipsychotics.
Berman et al., J Clin Psychiatry 2007 – adjunctive aripiprazole improved response in MDD inadequately responsive to antidepressants.
Report uncontrollable urges (gambling, shopping, eating, sexual)
Restlessness (akathisia) is common early – report it
Store below 30°C in a dry place, protected from light and moisture. Keep out of the reach of children. Do not use after the expiry date.
